Technology is what happens when a creature's picture of the world gets accurate enough that it stops merely *navigating* the world and starts *redirecting* it. Once you can predict what a change will do, the same understanding you used to find your way can be turned to remaking your surroundings. Its grown-up form moves the mental map outside the body altogether (into writing, notation, instruments, computers, the internet) where it can be stored, shared, queried, and recombined far beyond what any one head can hold. This is reach turned outward, not a rising above nature: the builder remaking the world is still a part of the world, working from no outside vantage. Tools and machines, on this view, are the same modeling activity carried on in shared matter.

::: {.identification}
**Technology** · *Identification*

Technology is the inside model turned *operative* on the structure it tracks: once an agent's modal field (§8.3) is accurate enough to predict the consequences of an alteration, the same recursion that navigated structure begins to redirect it. Its developed form externalizes the field into shared substrate (notation, instruments, computers), modal structure held outside any one body, persistent, queryable, recombinable. The agent redirecting structure is itself an agent within structure, operating from no exterior position; technology is reach turned outward, not a standing above Nature.
*Status: an identity claim on the §7.8 self-modeling structure (Principle 5), defended by fit, not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

Language (§8.10) was already a technology: the technology of shared interiority. Technology in the broader material sense generalizes that operation past the communicative register.

A self-modeling being with sufficient awareness has a model of the structure it inhabits. The model serves navigation and redirection. *Navigation*: anticipating what structure will do, aligning action with what is possible, taking what structure offers. *Redirection*: using the model to alter what structure produces. Reasoning, knowledge, meaning, will, and language all involve navigation, while language already begins redirection in the communicative register. Technology generalizes redirection into the material register.

The depth at which the second function opens is the depth at which the being has, jointly, a model accurate enough to predict consequences of alterations and the agentive self-modeling required to commit to alterations as projects rather than as impulses. Both are reached at roughly the same level of recursive depth: where the self-model integrates anticipatory simulation with goal-directed planning.

Animal tool use exists in shallow forms that lack one or both of these. Sea otters use stones to crack shellfish through learned association without sustained planning. Chimps termite-fish through behavioral routines that involve some anticipation but limited innovation across generations. New Caledonian crows manufacture and modify tools (Emery and Clayton 2004), closer to deep technology in planning and innovation, though without language to transmit refinement cumulatively. *Cumulative cultural technology* (tools used to make tools, refined across generations, taught between members and inherited) emerges most fully in humans, who have both the recursive depth required for cumulative refinement and the linguistic capacity to transmit knowledge across time. The depth gradient runs from learned association through planning through cumulative culture, and what tracks it is the level of awareness the organism has reached.

Technology is therefore a structural consequence of awareness-at-depth rather than a late achievement added to consciousness: the recursion turning from tracking to redirecting at the depth where its model becomes accurate enough to support alteration. A being at that depth produces technology under the conditions ordinarily required for it: opportunity, materials, social transmission, sufficient time. This is a convergence claim, not a strict modal entailment from the proof: the recursion turning operative on what it tracks is what the depth gradient makes available, while specific instantiations remain conditional on what the lineage's history and circumstances afford.

*The Inversion.* The standard reading treats technology as instrumental: a tool of survival extending biological needs into the social-historical realm. The framework reads it differently. Technology is the being's outward operation: the inside model turned operative on the structure it tracks. The being redirecting structure is itself a being within structure, operating from no exterior position, using its model to alter what structure produces, which is what dissipative beings have always done, now at a depth that includes itself in what it modulates.

*Externalization and the modal network.* The outward operation has a particular form worth marking. The framework's *externalization of the field* names the operation behind what philosophy-of-technology and cognitive-science literatures have approached under several rubrics: external representations (Zhang and Norman 1994), cognitive artifacts (Norman 1991), distributed cognition (Hutchins 1995), extended cognition (Clark and Chalmers 1998), and material inscriptions (Latour 1986); the framework names them by their modal-mapping function rather than by their representational vehicle, and adds that the operation externalizes the modal field §8.3 derives: what those literatures track as representational substrate is, on the framework's reading, the field held in shared matter. The being's inside model is its modal representation, its body-internal registration of the modal field (§8.3): what is, what is conditionally so, and what could be otherwise. Technology, at depth, is the *externalization* operation on the field: substrate configured to instantiate the field's modal structure outside the body, persistent across the reasoning interval, queryable, recombinable, transmissible across beings. Externalization makes the field shareable in a way no individual modal representation can be: what one body holds as its interior reading of the field becomes substrate other bodies can read, query, and recombine, and the field that was previously coextensive with each body's interior now extends across matter the body did not have to be. Technology can make a field of knowledge external, persistent, and available to many users: lodged in shared substrate rather than in any one private representation. Theorem 9 (Modal Convergence, §8.3) remains the narrower epistemic theorem of collectively held knowledge; externalization gives that knowledge a durable material support, rather than itself constituting a further application of the theorem. Notation, writing, mathematical formalism, instruments, and computers form a depth gradient of externalization, each stage lodging more of the field in shared substrate — the accreting *modal network*. The same operation runs across all of them: modal structure held in shared substrate (T, S, Φ: the structural roles derived in §§2.6–2.7 via the identification of the modal constraint with T∧S∧Φ and the Conditions-as-Nature work) at higher resolution than the unaided self-modeling subject can hold internally. The portability is not coincidence. Interior representations and their externalizations are configurations of one Nature; what permits a computation in silicon to substitute for one in neurons is that both are configurations of the same structural conditions. Computers are the most flexible externalization currently available, but the operation they instantiate is what cumulative cultural technology has been doing all along: extending the modal-mapping reach of the being beyond what any single body can hold.

*Standardization as interoperability.* Externalized knowledge coordinates action only where different people, instruments, and systems can read one another's representations. Shared technical standards reduce the translation work required at those boundaries. Measurement is a clear case. A decimal system allows many conversions to be inferred from one rule, while a system built from unrelated ratios requires more separate facts to be learned and retained. In mechanics, manufacturing, medicine, science, and transportation, incompatible standards can also duplicate tools, complicate training, and create opportunities for conversion error. The specialist can master that complexity, but mastery does not show that the complexity is necessary; expertise is better spent on the real complexity of the object than on avoidable friction in the language used to describe and maintain it. This supports interoperability, not cultural uniformity. A common public standard can govern the domains that must coordinate while customary units remain available in ordinary life. Whether a particular standard reduces errors, training time, and duplicated equipment is an empirical question; the argument identifies the function to test, not the answer in advance.

*The internet and AI as modal network.* Two contemporary configurations of the modal network warrant marking by name. The internet is the modal network at civilizational scale: substrate configured to instantiate, simultaneously, the modal holdings of very many bodies, readable and queryable across them — many individual fields pooled and interlinked into one shared body. Where individual writing and individual instruments extended a single body's modal representation, the internet extends the aggregated modal holdings of a civilization. The accuracy of what it represents depends entirely on the filtering apparatus between contributing bodies and shared substrate. With no filtering, the field carries the noise of every body that contributes, including lines the field never actually contained, dressed as lines it does. With strong filtering, it approaches what its best contributors hold. Social-epistemology accounts (Goldman, *Knowledge in a Social World* 1999; Origgi, *Reputation* 2018; Coady, *Testimony* 1992) describe the filtering apparatus a modal network requires if it is to function as knowledge rather than as noise. Large language models, trained on substantial slices of that aggregated substrate, are compressions of the modal network: they surface lines the inquiring body would not have hit alone and aggregate across more contributors than any individual could survey, while inheriting the underlying field's noise and adding compression artifacts of their own: confident assertions on contested questions, generated lines the field never contained, smoothed-out disputes that look like consensus only because the training process flattens them (Bender et al. 2021; Ji et al. 2023). The structural point is that AI is continuous with the prior gradient of externalization, not a break from it, and the user's filtering apparatus must do work on AI output that it would not have to do on a direct corpus query.

*Responsible use constrains amplified reach.* The ethical problem is not intelligence or technical power as such. It is amplified reach detached from purpose, restraint, review, and answerability. A responsible use identifies what the system is being asked to accomplish, limits what it may decide or do, preserves ways to inspect and correct the result, and leaves a person or institution answerable for the consequences. These requirements increase with the use's scale, stakes, authority, and irreversibility. A playful image made for friends and an automated decision governing healthcare, employment, political speech, or physical force do not require the same level of constraint.

*Assistance and substitution differ.* AI assists inquiry when it expands a person's ability to ask, compare, verify, revise, or create. It substitutes for inquiry when it supplies a result the nominal author cannot reconstruct, evaluate, or answer for. Play remains a legitimate use; purpose need not mean economic productivity. The relevant failure is unattended generation at scale: output produced without proportionate judgment or responsibility whose costs of evaluation, correction, storage, and attention are shifted onto everyone who encounters it. Cheap generation becomes information-environment extraction when the generator captures the benefit of volume while the public bears the work of determining whether anything produced is reliable or worth receiving.

*The device paradigm and the disburdening ledger.* Borgmann (1984) names a distinction the exterior-modal-maps gradient leaves implicit, not one it cannot carry. A *device* delivers a commodity while concealing the machinery that produces it; a *focal thing* delivers it through visible engagement that carries skill, attention, and relation as constituents of the activity rather than as overhead to be eliminated. A microwave meal and a meal cooked from scratch both deliver food; only the second is a focal practice. But both are externalizations of the field, and the distinction Borgmann marks is not between technology and something outside it; it is between two things an externalization can do to the practice that held the modeling: retire it or preserve it. That is a real axis the gradient as stated does not register, and the structural account gains rather than loses by marking it: the gradient measures reach, and Borgmann's distinction measures what a given gain in reach retires. Read through the drive (§8.1), the two are not opposed. Disburdenment frees a subject from spending itself on already-met needs and so opens modal-field reach, which is gain; but reach and depth are distinct axes, and an externalization that delivers the commodity while retiring the focal practice expands what is available to the body without deepening what the body can itself do. The curiosity drive §8.1 names persists through disburdenment rather than lapsing with it, which is why the device-form *captures* engagement rather than abolishing it: the same SEEKING orientation that would deepen a skill can instead be fed cheap proxy-data that simulates field-expansion without delivering a well-weighted field: the structural shape §8.1 already flags as an over-expanded field with unreliable weighting. Whether externalization becomes a gain or a hollowing depends on two things, neither supplied by the technology alone: first, whether capability and control are broadly distributed rather than concentrated in hidden machinery; second, whether people retain the practices §8.1 names — source evaluation, deliberate pruning, and focal practice — that turn expanded reach into deeper understanding rather than passive dependence on a device. *Holding On to Reality* (1999) carries the point into the digital register, where it is sharpest: read structurally, it identifies a real transformation in the texture and cost of engagement that digital externalization brings, not a break in the continuity of what technology is. The continuity claim survives as an account of what technology structurally *is*; what Borgmann adds is the ledger the celebratory reading omits: that every externalization disburdening a body of some modeling also retires the practice that held it, and whether the trade is gain is settled by arrangement and cultivation, not by the fact of continuity alone.

That same book sharpens the device/focal-thing distinction into a trichotomy worth engaging directly: natural information (a thing disclosing its own structure), cultural information (structure carried through skilled practice and tradition), and technological information (structure detached from any particular referent, freely substitutable, apt to be treated as reality's replacement rather than reality's report). The worry generalizes the disburdening ledger into a metaphysical substitution: a civilization saturated in technological information comes to treat the sign as the thing. On the framework here that substitution cannot go all the way down, because technological information is never a replacement *for* structure; it is structure (T, S, Φ) held in a different substrate, per the identification the externalization account already makes. What the trichotomy tracks correctly is not a threat to structure's reality but a threat to a practice: natural and cultural information carry engagement as a constituent of accessing structure, while technological information can be consumed without any of that engagement, which is the disburdening ledger's point restated at the register of information itself, not a further metaphysical cost beyond it.

The methodological result, developed for the fine-tuning case in §5.1.5: within a fixed modal frame, externalizations amplify the resolution at which the frame can be searched, simulated, and computed; they do not fix the frame. Frame-fixing remains a conceptual operation. A being armed with a very powerful modal network can compute very precise answers within whatever frame is supplied; whether the frame is well-formed for the question is not something the network can settle.

Before the subsection breakdown, one rival account warrants engagement here. The standard instrumentalist account treats technology as a means: a tool extending biological needs, evaluated by what it accomplishes for the organism that wields it. The framework concedes the instrumentalist's central observation: that technology does, in fact, extend biological functions, and that at the level of a single tool the means/end analysis is correct as far as it goes. What it misses is the structural conditions that make instrumental use available at all: the recursive depth required for a being to model the gap between what is and what could be, and to commit to closing the gap as a project. Technology is not less instrumental on this reading; it is what becomes possible when the recursion has reached the depth at which instrumental use is the kind of thing a being can do. The instrumentalist describes the activity correctly and locates its conditions wrongly.
